articles.title: A kitchen to be proud of this Christmas: meet Rochdale’s family-run SJF Granite & Quartz
articles.excerpt: With 25 years of experience and a reported 124 five-star reviews, this local family business puts craftsmanship and personal service at the heart of its work.
articles.content_html:
With 25 years of experience and a reported 124 five-star reviews, this local family business puts craftsmanship and personal service at the heart of its work.

Christmas has a way of bringing everyone into the kitchen. From preparing the festive dinner to catching up over a drink, it becomes the busiest—and often happiest—room in the house.

For anyone dreaming of giving that space a beautiful new finish, Rochdale’s SJF Granite & Quartz Ltd offers local expertise with a personal touch.

The family-owned business specialises in bespoke granite and quartz surfaces, serving homes and businesses across Rochdale, Greater Manchester and surrounding areas. Its website highlights 25 years of experience and a commitment to quality, precision and value for money.

Behind every attractive worktop is careful workmanship. SJF describes a process that takes projects from detailed measurement and templating through to cutting, polishing and installation—bringing the individual elements together into a finished surface tailored to the space.

The reported tally of 124 five-star reviews adds an encouraging chapter to this local family-business story. Choosing someone to work in your home is a matter of trust, and recommendations from previous customers can be an important part of that decision.

SJF places personal service at the centre of its approach, alongside carefully crafted stone and competitive pricing. It is a combination with clear appeal for homeowners who want their kitchen to feel special while keeping their budget in mind.

With Christmas approaching, now is a good time to start discussing the kitchen you have been imagining. Choosing a surface, exploring samples and arranging measurements early gives you time to consider the details and ask about installation availability before the festive season.

Whether your plans involve a complete kitchen renovation or replacing existing worktops, a beautifully chosen surface can become the detail that brings the room together.

SJF’s showroom at 47 Church Street, Littleborough, OL15 8AB offers the opportunity to explore samples. Its website also showcases completed projects and provides a free quotation enquiry form.

For inspiration, project enquiries and Christmas availability, visit https://sjfgraniteandquartz.co.uk/ or call 07311 133375.

Your dream kitchen could start with a conversation—and a family business right here in the Rochdale borough.

articles.title: Pacific, Mangos and Empire until morning: remembering Rochdale’s strip
articles.excerpt: Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—remembering Rochdale’s strip, its familiar faces and the venues keeping the town alive today.
articles.content_html:
Box-dye red hair, Jägerbombs and taxi queues that lasted hours—Rochdale’s nightlife in the 2000s and early 2010s was a whole chapter of growing up. And places such as Empire are still helping the town make memories.

There was a time when a night out in Rochdale came with its own wardrobe, soundtrack and familiar faces.

Box-dye red hair. Chinos. Ed Hardy. The infamous Rihanna jumper. Outfits that, looking back, were remarkably close to business casual—worn with complete confidence for a night on the strip.

Rihanna and Eminem provided the soundtrack. Ordering a Jägerbomb felt like an event. Pacific, Mangos, Litten Tree and Empire were names woven into the weekend.

Between the bars, the dancefloors and the eventual search for a taxi, Rochdale felt wonderfully alive.

One former glass collector and barmaid remembers an incredible scene: heaving venues, wonderful bouncers and, in her experience, few fights. When the night finally ended, queues for taxis could mean waiting for hours into the early morning.

The people who made the strip

Ask someone about their old nights out and they might start with a club. Before long, they will be talking about a person.

A favourite barmaid. A reassuring face on the door. Someone you always bumped into, whether you had arranged to meet or not.

Among those familiar faces was the man affectionately known to revellers as “the gas man”, remembered sitting at the corner of the strip.

The former bar worker recalls people stopping to hug him and give him money. Despite the difficult circumstances she remembers him facing, he was a beloved presence, recognised and greeted with affection.

His circumstances were his own, and a nickname cannot tell his whole story. But the warmth with which he is remembered belongs in the history of those nights, alongside the music and the venues.

The strip’s character came from its people.

From the glass collector’s side of the dancefloor

Working through those nights meant seeing what customers sometimes missed.

Collecting glasses through a crowded room. Keeping the bar moving. Watching the door team manage another wave of arrivals while friends tried to find one another inside.

The former worker remembers the bouncers warmly. Her account offers a different perspective from the assumption that a busy nightlife scene must have been defined by trouble: what stays with her is how enjoyable it was, how few fights she encountered and how much life filled the town centre.

That is a personal recollection, rather than a claim that every night passed without incident. But it captures something worth preserving—the pleasure of working somewhere everyone wanted to be.

What happened to Pacific, Mangos and Litten Tree?

Pacific, at 8 South Parade, is now listed as closed. An archived council entry records a premises-licence suspension beginning in July 2013 for non-payment of an annual fee or levy. That record does not, by itself, establish the venue’s final trading date or the full reasons it closed.

Sources: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/204/Detail?APP_ID=80078 and https://www.pubsgalore.co.uk/areas/rochdale-central/greater-manchester/

Mangos’ connection to a later venue remains visible in the paperwork. The council’s licensing record for Trinity retains conditions referring to the operating plan for Mango Bar at 3 King Street. The familiar address acquired another identity, although the sources reviewed do not establish the complete changeover story.

Source: https://licensing.rochdale.gov.uk/1/LicensingActPremises/Search/203/Detail?LIC_ID=6700

Litten Tree’s premises at 10 Fleece Street subsequently became Yates and are now Courtyard Rochdale. CAMRA records its reopening under the Courtyard name in March 2024. For former regulars, the sign has changed, but the address remains somewhere people can meet for a night out.

Source: https://camra.org.uk/pubs/courtyard-rochdale-rochdale-153361

Empire: the night that kept going

Then there was Empire.

In the former bar worker’s memories, it was the infamous destination where the night could stretch towards 6am. Leaving meant discovering that the early morning had arrived while everyone was still enjoying themselves.

Empire remains part of Rochdale’s nightlife today. Its presently advertised Friday and Saturday hours run until 4am, with live bands and performances central to its programme.

Source: https://empirerochdale.co.uk/

Its contribution extends beyond an ordinary weekend. The council’s 2026 Feel Good Festival programme included performances throughout the day at Empire, followed by a midnight DJ slot.

Source: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/rochdale-feel-good-festival/indoor-venues

That continuing activity deserves recognition. Venues such as Empire give people a reason to come into Rochdale, meet friends, hear music and spend an evening in their own town.

The old strip cannot be recreated exactly. Its customers have grown older; their wardrobes, responsibilities and stamina may have changed.

But the affection remains—for the songs, the people, the staff who looked after everyone and the nights nobody wanted to finish.

Rochdale’s next great night out needs people willing to make it happen. Empire and the town’s other active venues are keeping that possibility alive.

What do you remember about the strip? Pacific or Mangos? Litten Tree before Empire? The Rihanna jumper, the Jägerbombs or the seemingly endless taxi queue? Share your memories—and give a mention to the bar staff, glass collectors and door teams who made those nights special.

articles.title: Rochdale Council to Decide on Housing Development in Bamford Next Week
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council's planning committee will reconvene on October 22 to make a decision on a proposed housing development on former playing fields in Bamford, following concerns over drainage and transport connectivity.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council's planning committee is set to reconvene on Thursday, October 22, to decide the fate of a proposed housing development on former playing fields in Bamford. The decision was previously delayed in August due to concerns regarding drainage and transport connectivity.

The development, proposed by Wain Homes, aims to build 45 houses on a plot of land behind Greenvale. The site, located to the west of Norden Road, has a history of flooding, prompting the committee to seek further details from the developers about drainage measures before proceeding with the application.

Councillor Tom Besford expressed concerns about the lack of an overall masterplan for the site, warning that piecemeal developments could lead to insufficient affordable housing and inadequate infrastructure. The committee's hesitation reflects a broader apprehension about the implications of the development on local amenities and transport links.

If approved, this project would mark the first phase of a larger scheme that could see up to 450 homes built on the site, which was removed from green belt status under the Greater Manchester housing strategy, Places for Everyone. The overarching plan includes the construction of a new clubhouse for Bridge FC and improved sports pitches, which are seen as potential benefits of the development.

articles.title: Where Rochdale’s next homes are planned—and who can afford them
articles.excerpt: Our investigation examines 22 housing developments and regeneration plans across Rochdale borough: homes, prices, affordable tenure, land, school places, GP capacity and transport funding.
articles.content_html:
The homes are planned, but will Rochdale get the housing its residents need?

Rochdale’s housing pipeline spans large farmland neighbourhoods, former industrial and retail sites, and replacement of existing social housing. The schemes are at different stages. Allocated land, a committee resolution, a formal permission, a construction start and an occupied home are not interchangeable.

How many homes is Rochdale expected to deliver?

The council’s 2026 housing topic paper uses the adopted Places for Everyone requirement of 10,472 net additional homes in 2022–2039: 568 annually in 2022–2025, 616 in 2025–2030 and 632 in 2030–2039. It records 650 net additions in 2024/25, above that year’s 568 requirement. This is historical performance, not proof of delivery in 2026/27.

Does the pipeline meet the government’s target?

The answer is qualified. The 2025 land assessment identifies sufficient potential supply against the adopted plan benchmark, but availability forecasts do not guarantee completions. National housing need is a separate calculation, using housing stock and affordability. The current national framework was issued in August 2026; older council estimates of the revised need are not interchangeable with a freshly calculated October figure. The latest annual delivery, current standard-method calculation and appropriate land-supply buffer still need confirmation before claiming the borough meets every present national requirement.

Why affordable numbers matter

The May 2026 housing-needs assessment estimates a net annual affordable shortfall of 768 homes under a ten-year backlog-clearance model. That is an assessment of need, not a separate statutory annual building quota, and includes the role of existing stock. Appendix C contains the detailed calculation; its headline gross figures are internally inconsistent, so this series uses the consistent net figure. The distinction is essential: meeting an overall housing target does not automatically meet the needs of households who cannot afford market homes.

What does affordable mean?

Social Rent is set under government rent policy. Other affordable rental products are regulated or discounted against local rents. Shared ownership and discounted sale help eligible purchasers but still involve household costs. For each scheme, actual rent, purchase price, unowned-share rent, service charges, estate fees and eligibility are the useful affordability evidence. A marketing incentive or a claim that a property is cheaper than Manchester does not establish planning-defined affordability.

Green Belt and brownfield are different questions

Green Belt is a planning designation; greenfield and brownfield describe the land and its development history. Agricultural fields can have been removed from the Green Belt while remaining greenfield. Brownfield can also lie within Green Belt. The quarry’s restoration history and the precise development boundary matter. “Brown belt” is not the equivalent planning category.

Do stronger Green Belt affordable rules apply to these schemes?

Current policy GB8 includes affordable provision, infrastructure and accessible green space. Its footnote 43 excludes development on land released through plans adopted before 12 December 2024, and permissions on Green Belt granted before that date. Places for Everyone was adopted in March 2024. It would therefore be misleading to say every listed former Green Belt allocation automatically requires 50% affordable housing. The actual site, date of release, permission and obligations must be checked.

Can infrastructure cope?

The August 2026 infrastructure document is a scoping assessment and coordination framework. It discusses assessment, funding and healthcare planning; it is not proof that every scheme already has funded school places, staffed GP capacity or completed drainage works. The defensible borough-wide conclusion is that support depends on scheme-specific evidence and delivery. This review does not establish that infrastructure either universally supports or universally fails the housing programme.

What evidence would settle the question?

For each scheme, residents need the current decision notice, executed Section 106 agreement, condition-discharge records, affordable tenure schedule and occupation triggers. Infrastructure evidence should cover cumulative traffic, schools including SEND, NHS primary care, drainage and sewer capacity, utilities, public transport, biodiversity and maintenance. A payment or reserved school plot is not the same as an operational service.

Why there is no grand total for these articles

Several entries overlap: Northstone is within South Heywood; Foundry Fields implements the Roch Valley allocation; Barratt’s Stakehill application is within a larger allocation. Lower Falinge replaces existing homes. Completed plots and care-home beds need different treatment. Adding every headline number would produce a misleading total.

Scope and evidence date

Research checked 14 October 2026. This series covers 22 identified major development and regeneration topics across Rochdale borough. It is not a census of every small planning application. Some developments already have occupied homes; asking prices are snapshots. The articles will be updated when outstanding information becomes available.

Secured money, receipts and spending are different

The council’s 2024/25 Infrastructure Funding Statement records £1,522,730 secured through new agreements and £1,629,989 received from agreements across the borough. Of education receipts that year, £619,533 was allocated and none yet spent; separately, £417,976 of older education contributions was spent. It would be false to say no education money was spent. The summary does not identify each development’s payments, school places or occupation triggers. It lists new agreements for Hawks View and Silver Hill, but cannot replace their full signed deeds.

The school forecast is an assessment, not an opening guarantee

The December 2025 primary-school report forecasts Heywood Reception surpluses of 34 in 2026/27, 61 in 2027/28, 29 in 2028/29 and five in 2029/30, with South Heywood housing and school timing to be monitored. For Middleton it forecasts 28 extra places needed in 2026/27, then surpluses of 40, 71 and nine. It discusses additional classes, including use of an existing Hollins classroom; this review does not establish a development-specific approved capital budget or new-school opening from those forecasts. Forecasts are dated planning estimates, not live admissions availability or proof of spare secondary/SEND capacity.

Pennines capacity and the healthcare warning

The school-plan appendix reports, at its assessment date, 75 spare Reception places in North Pennines and 25 in South Pennines, plus 303 spare Key Stage 1 places. Those area figures cannot be treated as guaranteed capacity beside every new estate. For Simister/Bowlee, the NHS’s September 2026 response identifies existing constraints at nearby practices and ongoing assessments, without publishing a funded expansion timetable. Infrastructure support therefore requires more than the existence of nearby schools, surgeries or stations.

Further information and updates

Some final planning agreements, exact rents and prices, affordable-housing breakdowns and infrastructure funding details are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. The relevant articles will be updated when the information becomes available.

articles.title: Volunteers and council team tackle overgrown areas at Middleton’s Jubilee Park
articles.excerpt: The Friends of Jubilee Park and council staff have joined forces for the second phase of work to manage overgrown shrubs and care for the park’s rhododendrons.
articles.content_html:
Work to open up overgrown shrub areas at Jubilee Park in Middleton has entered its second phase, with volunteers and council staff joining forces to improve the grounds.

The Friends of Jubilee Park have been working alongside Rochdale Borough Council’s Environmental Management team, carrying out maintenance that includes caring for the park’s collection of rhododendrons.

The group says the work will encourage healthy new growth over the next couple of seasons, improve views and sight lines, and help visitors feel safer.

Opening up densely planted areas is intended to create a brighter, more welcoming park while supporting the long-term health of its shrubs.

Visitors may notice that some sections look temporarily untidy as the work progresses. The Friends have asked for patience, explaining that the maintenance is intended to bring lasting improvements.

“These improvements will bring lasting benefits for visitors and help Jubilee Park continue to thrive,” the group said.

The Friends describe Jubilee Park as a Gold Medal-winning Green Flag park and thanked visitors for their understanding while volunteers and staff care for the grounds.

The latest work forms part of an ongoing effort to maintain the much-loved Middleton green space for everyone who uses it.

Source: Friends of Jubilee Park update supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Inclusive roundabout and zip line feature in plans for new Falinge Park play area
articles.excerpt: Mayoress Iram Faisal has unveiled plans for new play equipment at Falinge Park, including a wheelchair-accessible roundabout, an inclusive seesaw and a double cableway zip line.
articles.content_html:
Plans for a new play area at Falinge Park have been unveiled, with wheelchair-accessible equipment among the attractions proposed for children and families.

Mayoress Iram Faisal shared details of the project, describing it as a deeply personal undertaking in the park where she played as a child.

The proposed equipment includes a double cableway zip line with ramps; a toddler multi-play unit; toddler and junior swings; an inclusive seesaw; a Crazy Gander springer; and a wheelchair-accessible roundabout.

In her announcement, Mrs Faisal said inclusivity had been central to the vision, with the aim of helping more children enjoy the park together.

“Every child deserves the opportunity to play, explore and enjoy their childhood,” she said.

For the Mayoress, the plans also carry memories of her own upbringing.

“Having lived here and played in this very park myself, to now be in a position to play a part in transforming it for the next generation has been an incredibly emotional journey,” she said.

She thanked councillors Faisal Rana and Amber Nisa, Rochdale Borough Council and its Environmental Management Team, alongside everyone involved in bringing the project forward.

Mrs Faisal said the improvements were about investing in children and creating a space where families could make memories together.

“From playing in Falinge Park as a child to helping shape its future, this really is a full-circle moment,” she added.

The announcement refers to a hoped-for start towards the end of February, with work continuing into March, subject to final arrangements. It does not specify the year or confirm an opening date, so that timetable remains to be clarified.

Residents have been invited to share their views on the proposals.

Source: announcement by Mayoress Iram Faisal, supplied to Rochdale Daily and published on her public Facebook page: https://www.facebook.com/iram.faisal.5095/posts/1764829918060894/

articles.title: Emmerdale star Lisa Riley meets shoppers as Peacocks opens in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store on Thursday, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.
articles.content_html:
Peacocks opened its new Rochdale Riverside store today, with Emmerdale star Lisa Riley joining the celebrations and posing for photographs with shoppers.

The actress helped officially launch the branch on Thursday 15 October, cutting the ribbon alongside store manager Claire Kershaw and the shop team. Riley also celebrated the visit on her own social media, confirming she had opened the new store.

Her appearance gave shoppers an opportunity to meet a familiar television face while exploring the retailer’s latest addition to Rochdale town centre.

Customers were keen to get through the doors, with the first shopper reportedly arriving at 6.30am. The first ten customers each received a £50 Peacocks gift card.

The new branch stocks clothing for women, men and children, bringing Peacocks back to the town following the closure of its former Wheatsheaf Shopping Centre shop in 2020.

For residents pleased to see the name return, today was a chance to browse the new shop, meet its staff and enjoy a little soap-star glamour alongside their shopping.

Sources: Roch Valley Radio’s opening-day report: https://www.rochvalleyradio.com/news-features/140/business/1040/lisa-riley-opens-new-peacocks-store-at-rochdale-riverside Lisa Riley’s public opening announcement: https://www.facebook.com/officiallisariley/posts/1657501805737969/ Shoppers’ photographs: information supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Announces Free Bonfire Night Events for November 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council will host three free firework displays across the borough in early November, featuring reduced noise fireworks for accessibility.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council has confirmed a series of free firework displays to celebrate Bonfire Night in November 2026. The events will take place at three locations across the borough, including Middleton, Heywood, and Syke, with festivities beginning on Monday, November 2.

The first event will be held at Bowlee Community Park, located on Heywood Old Road in Middleton, starting at 6pm. The bonfire will be lit at 7pm, followed by fireworks at 7.30pm. The second display will occur on Tuesday, November 3, at Queen’s Park Road in Heywood, with the same timings. The final council-run event will take place on Thursday, November 4, at Cronkeyshaw Common in Syke, also starting at 6pm.

In addition to the council events, Milnrow Cricket Club and Lobden Golf Club in Whitworth will host their own firework displays on Saturday, November 7. The Milnrow event will charge £7 for adults and £11.25 for families, while the Lobden Golf Club display will cost £5 for adults and £3 for children.

Rochdale Council has introduced reduced noise fireworks this year to make the displays more accessible for all attendees. The council advises visitors to walk or use public transport due to limited parking at the venues. Alcohol, fireworks, and sparklers are prohibited at all council-run events, and no toilet facilities will be available.

articles.title: Rochdale's Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre Set to Drive Advanced Manufacturing
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre at Kingsway Business Park marks a significant step for Rochdale's advanced manufacturing sector, with operations expected to commence in 2027.
articles.content_html:
A major milestone has been reached with the completion of the base build of the Sustainable Materials & Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) at Kingsway Business Park in Rochdale. This 30,000 sq. ft facility is poised to become a key player in the UK's advanced materials and manufacturing sector, serving as a gateway for innovation and collaboration within the region.

The SMMC is the first significant development within the Atom Valley Innovation District (AVID), a 25-acre hub designed to foster advanced materials and manufacturing. The centre aims to bring together businesses, researchers, investors, and innovation partners, enhancing Greater Manchester's reputation as a leading centre for advanced manufacturing.

The completion of the building is the result of extensive collaboration among various stakeholders, including the Rochdale Development Agency (RDA), Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA), and The University of Manchester. The next phase will involve transitioning from construction to specialist fit-out, with the centre expected to commence operations in 2027.

Since the establishment of the Centre of Expertise in Advanced Materials and Sustainability (CEAMS) in 2023, over 90 companies have engaged with the initiative, benefiting from access to a national network of expertise and support. This development is expected to significantly contribute to the growth of the advanced manufacturing sector in Rochdale and beyond.

articles.title: Did Robin Hood really come to Healey Dell?
articles.excerpt: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.summary: Local stories tie a lost ring, witches and a 'Fairy Chapel' to Robin Hood — the tales are colourful, but what do the records actually show?
articles.body:
There is a pulpit-shaped rock, a narrow pool and a name — the Fairy Chapel — at the base of Healey Dell’s steep gorge. The visitor centre and local heritage guides record a set of vivid stories: a King of the Fairies who turned a coven to stone, a ring lost in the river that cost a would‑be heir his title, and an origin tale that sends “Robert of Huntingdon” on the road to becoming Robin Hood. These versions are the ones you’ll see on site interpretation and in the Heritage Centre’s write‑ups. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

That is folklore, not archival evidence. The most systematic scholarly account of the Dell is an archaeological desk‑based assessment carried out for Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council by the University of Manchester Archaeological Unit in December 2004. It maps the valley’s mills, lodges, railway viaduct and later Victorian and industrial remains; it lists the local archives and printed sources consulted (John Rylands, Lancashire Record Office, Rochdale Local Studies and others) and documents the Dell’s long industrial and landscape history — but it does not produce contemporary medieval records linking a historical Robin Hood or a Robert of Huntingdon to Healey Dell. Put bluntly: the detailed desk‑based study records place, industry and later antiquarian interest, not a medieval outlaw’s itinerary. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

Healey Dell’s real, verifiable past is useful and interesting in itself. The site is a designated local nature reserve and a managed visitor attraction, with a Victorian railway viaduct that is Grade II listed and the valley’s surviving mill archaeology. Rochdale Borough Council describes the reserve, the visitor centre’s pictorial displays and the family‑oriented Fairy Grotto as part of the attraction visitors can find at Dell Road, Healey. The viaduct and the visible industrial remains are the kinds of things that the archaeological assessment and Historic England record in statutory listings. ([rochdale.gov.uk](https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/737/healey-dell-nature-reserve-and-tea-rooms-rochdale))

How did the Robin Hood story arrive here? Local legends often accrete around striking landscape features; caverns, pools and ravines attract tales of fairies, witches and enchanted tokens across Britain. The Healey Dell accounts appear in local storytelling and modern retellings by the Heritage Centre and local guides: they make no claim to derive from contemporary medieval documents but preserve a late tradition tying a Huntingdon name and a lost ring to the Chapel. Those popular accounts are part of the Dell’s cultural history and of local imaginative life — important for tourism and local identity — but they do not equal documentary proof. ([healeydelltearooms.co.uk](https://www.healeydelltearooms.co.uk/things-to-do/the-fairies-chapel/))

On the bigger question of Robin Hood’s historicity, mainstream scholarship treats Robin Hood as a legendary figure built from ballads and popular tales rather than a single, verifiable medieval person whose movements can be read off local court rolls. Modern reference works and folklorists stress the ballad tradition and its late medieval and post‑medieval formation; many local Robin Hood claims around England are later inventions, popular attributions or imaginative explanations for landscape oddities rather than recordable events. That does not make the stories worthless — it makes them folklore. ([books.google.com](https://books.google.com/books/about/Oxford_Dictionary_of_English_Folklore.html?hl=en&id=w2BMSAAACAAJ&output=html_text))

So what can a reader reasonably take away? If you mean “is there documentary, contemporary medieval evidence that Robin Hood or Robert of Huntingdon passed through Healey Dell?” the answer is: no such evidence has been produced in the local archival and archaeological surveys cited by the University of Manchester assessment and by the council’s heritage material. If you mean “are there stories that people tell about Robin Hood, witches and a magic ring here?” the answer is yes — they are recorded in local guides and on site interpretation, and they help make the place culturally lively. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

If you want to read more or check sources yourself: the University of Manchester archaeological desk‑based assessment (2004) is the most thorough published study of Healey Dell’s historic fabric; Rochdale Borough Council holds the reserve’s visitor information; the Healey Dell Heritage Centre publishes the Fairy Chapel story used in interpretation. None of these sources substitutes for a named medieval document placing Robin Hood in the Dell — and until such a record appears, the Robin Hood connection belongs to folklore rather than local history. ([rmnf.org.uk](https://www.rmnf.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Vol-1-Healey-Dell-Final-Report.pdf))

articles.title: Cozy Market in Milnrow Shut Down Again for Selling Illicit Tobacco
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Trading Standards has secured a three-month closure order for Cozy Market on Dale Street, Milnrow, due to the persistent sale of illegal tobacco products, just weeks after the shop reopened.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Trading Standards has successfully obtained a closure order for Cozy Market, located at 79 Dale Street in Milnrow, following the shop's continued sale of illicit tobacco products. The order was granted by Manchester Magistrates’ Court and will see the shop closed for three months.

This latest closure comes just weeks after Cozy Market reopened following a previous three-month closure order issued in June for similar violations. The council's trading standards team reported that illicit tobacco was seized as evidence during their investigations.

The law currently permits the closure of shops found selling illegal goods for a period of three months, but there are plans to extend this duration to a year. The council has reiterated its commitment to tackling the sale of illegal goods in the area.

Following the closure, Rochdale Council shared the news on social media, emphasising the importance of maintaining compliance with trading regulations. The council's actions aim to protect local communities from the negative impacts of illegal trading.

articles.excerpt: 39 dated Halloween listings across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Milnrow, Littleborough, Norden and Wardle, with prices, times, age suitability, venues and booking links.
articles.content_html:
From free family fun at the Town Hall and Empire to pool parties, pumpkin carving, costume competitions and late-night entertainment, here is our area-by-area guide to the spooky season.

Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October this year, but celebrations stretch across half-term and into Sunday 1 November. There are options for young children, teenagers, families and adults, including events advertised on local Facebook pages.

Find your area below. Listings run in date order within each area; events with several dates appear at their first date. Prices are the published figures available when checked. Where hours, age limits, admission charges or booking details remain unconfirmed, we say so.

This guide brings together the public 2026 announcements we could identify and check. Private groups, unadvertised parties and later announcements mean no guide can guarantee every event. Organisers can send additions to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

Find a plan quickly

Free family events: Town Hall, 26 October–1 November; Empire children’s party, 27 October.

Children’s parties: Rochdale RUFC, Milnrow and Littleborough cricket clubs, BizzyBees and Wardle Club. Check the age policies below.

Older children and teenagers: Younique Talent ages 7–17; Hollingworth Lake activity morning ages 8+; Monsters of Rock for accompanied ages 14+.

A party with a quiet room: Keeley B at Butterworth Hall on 30 October.

Adults: Norden workshops, Royal Toby bingo, Town Hall horror cinema and evening live music. Decadance is separately marked as an adults-only lifestyle venue.

articles.title: East Middleton councillor questions parking charge warning after petrol station breakdown
articles.excerpt: Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned about a parking charge while waiting for the RAC after her car broke down on Oldham Road.
articles.content_html:
Labour councillor Georgina Jacques says she was warned she could face a parking charge while waiting for recovery after her car broke down at a petrol station on Oldham Road.

Councillor Jacques, who represents East Middleton on Rochdale Borough Council, described the incident in a public Facebook post, asking whether the business could charge her when her vehicle would not start.

Writing about the breakdown, she said:

“So I’ve broken down in Petrol station on Oldham Road.

“Yes another car that’s absolutely useless ”

She then described a conversation with a member of staff:

“Anyway the guy working there said, I am gunna get charged for parking when his boss comes, as hes saying I can’t stay waiting for RAC!!! I can’t move my car obviously as it won’t start ”

According to her account, the vehicle was beside the station’s tyre inflation equipment. She wrote:

“it’s at the tyre pumper upper so not really blocking anywhere.

“So is this legal does anyone know surly they can’t charge me for breaking down.”

Councillor Jacques said the RAC had given her an estimated arrival window between 9.30pm and 11.30pm.

The screenshot does not establish that a parking charge was subsequently issued, how much was allegedly proposed, or which parking conditions applied. The petrol station is not named in the post, and its account of the conversation is not available.

Could she actually be charged?

A private parking operator can issue a parking charge where it alleges that a driver breached the site’s parking conditions. That is a civil payment demand, rather than a criminal charge. Whether a demand would be enforceable in this particular case cannot be determined from the Facebook post alone. The signage, terms, circumstances of the breakdown and evidence of the recovery arrangements would matter.

However, a breakdown gives a motorist a strong reason to challenge a ticket issued while waiting for repairs or recovery. Citizens Advice specifically identifies being unable to move a broken-down vehicle as grounds for an appeal. That does not guarantee automatic cancellation, but it means a demand should not simply be assumed valid.

Independent parking appeals service POPLA also identifies evidence of a breakdown and a recovery callout as relevant when exceptional circumstances prevented a driver from complying with parking conditions.

Drivers in this situation should retain recovery booking messages, attendance records and photographs of the parking signs. The Competition and Markets Authority advises motorists to preserve evidence when a breakdown occurs and to challenge a disputed charge rather than ignore it.

For now, Councillor Jacques’s post establishes that she reported being warned about a possible charge. It does not establish that she received one or that any payment was legally owed.

Sources: Facebook post attributed to Councillor Georgina Jacques, screenshot supplied to Rochdale Daily; council profile: https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7226; Citizens Advice: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/law-and-courts/parking-tickets/when-to-appeal-a-parking-ticket/; POPLA: https://www.popla.co.uk/appeal-guide; CMA: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/parking-charges-cma-takes-action-to-drive-improvements-for-motorists

We hope Councillor Jacques is rescued promptly and back to her council duties in the morning—with her car feeling rather more cooperative.

BREAKING NEWS — LIVE

17:54, 14 October 2026

A police operation has led to the arrest of seventeen individuals as officers tackle an organised crime group linked to violent incidents earlier this year.

Seventeen people have been arrested as part of a police operation targeting an organised crime group in Rochdale and Heywood. The operation, named Operation Rivercrest, involved 250 officers executing 20 warrants across multiple locations, including Rochdale, Heywood, Bury, Salford, Manchester, Merseyside, and Yorkshire.

The arrests, which took place on the morning of October 14, include sixteen men aged between 19 and 49, who are suspected of various offences such as drug supply, assault, violent disorder, affray, burglary, and robbery. A 21-year-old woman was also arrested on suspicion of being involved in drug supply.

Detective Sergeant Hannah Taala from Greater Manchester Police’s Rochdale Division stated that the operation was initiated following a violent incident in Heywood earlier this year, which resulted in serious injuries, including a stabbing. She noted that the violence involved multiple individuals and the use of weapons, including machetes.

During the raids, a cannabis farm was discovered, highlighting the extent of the criminal activities being targeted. The police have not disclosed the next steps in the investigation, but the operation underscores ongoing efforts to dismantle organised crime networks in the area.

articles.title: Teenager Jailed for Fatal Crash in Middleton After Teaching Himself to Drive
articles.excerpt: An 18-year-old has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison after causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly.
articles.content_html:
A teenager has been sentenced to nearly seven years in prison for causing the death of a grandfather in Middleton while driving unlicensed and recklessly. Ruhul Islam, now 18, taught himself to drive by watching YouTube videos and was behind the wheel of his brother's Nissan Micra when he struck Terence James, 78, on Shawbury Street on September 29, 2024.

During a hearing at Manchester Crown Court on October 13, it was revealed that Islam had borrowed the car to make takeaway deliveries for a local business. Witnesses reported seeing him swerving through traffic, running red lights, and driving aggressively shortly before the crash. Mr James was crossing the road with his 10-year-old granddaughter when he was hit, suffering severe injuries that led to his death the following day after life support was withdrawn.

Judge Kate Cornell described the vehicle as a 'dangerous weapon' in the hands of someone unqualified to drive. She stated that Mr James would likely still be alive had Islam adhered to traffic laws. The court heard that Islam initially attempted to conceal his involvement in the crash, claiming his older brother was driving at the time.

The incident has raised concerns about road safety and the consequences of unlicensed driving. Following the sentencing, it is expected that discussions around stricter enforcement of driving regulations may take place, although no specific measures have been announced yet.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Announces New Regeneration Projects for Middleton
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has unveiled a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, including the restoration of Hopwood Hall and the acquisition of Warwick Mill.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced a series of regeneration projects aimed at revitalising Middleton, following a recent High Court judgement in favour of the council regarding Hopwood Hall. This decision brings clarity to the future of the historic building, which has seen over £1.6 million invested since 2017 by the council and Historic England. The council is committed to funding essential repairs and considering options for its long-term future.

In addition to the Hopwood Hall project, the council has made significant strides in Middleton's regeneration ambitions. The acquisition of Middleton Old Grammar School is expected to lead to the announcement of a new tenant before the end of the year. Furthermore, the council is in the process of acquiring the long-derelict Warwick Mill, which could be redeveloped for new housing, enhancing the local community.

Plans are also underway to transform the Middleton Scout Hut into a community venue that will provide activities and training opportunities for young people. The council has also confirmed that banking and post office services will return to Middleton town centre in the new year, a move that is anticipated to provide a boost to the local economy.

These initiatives are part of the council's broader commitment to invest in the borough, creating jobs and driving economic growth. The council has also approved a £15 million support package over the next three years to assist residents facing financial difficulties, ensuring that help is available for those in need.

The development framework includes a new primary school in the Bury portion, a local centre, a spine road, off-site highway works, active-travel routes, green infrastructure and drainage measures. These are requirements and ambitions for a future neighbourhood, rather than proof that all funding and construction contracts are in place.

Bury’s website cites its own affordable policy rate and an approximate affordable total for the Bury homes. That percentage should not be automatically applied to the Rochdale share. The eventual cross-boundary applications need clear tenure schedules and allocation arrangements.

Residents campaigning against the development raise traffic and drainage concerns. Those are attributed concerns, not verified findings that infrastructure cannot accommodate the plan. The published assessments and conditions must show how risks are addressed.

A specific Rochdale housebuilder and site-specific adverse legal finding have not been verified here. The employment-led Northern Gateway and residential Simister/Bowlee programme should also be kept distinct when explaining approvals.

The core accountability question is whether cross-border delivery provides the services residents actually use, with an enforceable timetable rather than separate promises by different authorities.

Planning stage: Strategic allocation; June 2026 development framework guides later applications

Affordable breakdown: 200 of the 1,550 homes are in Rochdale. The Bury affordable percentage must not be applied automatically to those 200; Rochdale-specific signed tenure counts are not established.

NHS Property Services is undertaking capacity assessments. The response provides no funded expansion budget, extra appointment/staffing figures or delivery date.

Eighty care-home beds cannot simply be added to twenty houses and advertised as one hundred ordinary family homes. Any contribution to the housing-delivery measure must use the applicable treatment of communal accommodation.

Access, staff and visitor travel, drainage and the relationship with nearby services are central infrastructure questions. No site-specific capacity assessment was verified here. The developer’s approval statement does not supply that evidence.

No verified adverse builder finding relating to this Middleton scheme was established. A planning dispute elsewhere, or a similarly named company, would not alone establish a problem with this development.

articles.content_html:
College Bank’s future cannot yet be presented as a confirmed number of new homes. RBH’s July 2026 update records that 100 customers had accepted offers of another home and 64 had moved from the high-rise blocks at that point.

That is evidence of rehousing progress at a particular date, not evidence that replacement homes have been constructed or that a final demolition or refurbishment programme is approved. Earlier reporting described continuing uncertainty over the solution for the Seven Sisters.

RBH says resident safety drives the move and that it is supporting tenants through the process. A complete account should include the position of residents who wish to stay, the available alternatives and any future right-to-return arrangements.

This is separate from the neighbouring Lower Falinge proposal. Combining the two without checking their boundaries and replacement totals risks overstating supply and obscuring the number of existing affordable homes temporarily or permanently lost.

The January 2026 regulator judgement recognises RBH’s governance improvement but identifies material risks around investment and regeneration. It is not a project approval or an assessment of whether demolition is the best option.

Until the final scheme is evidenced, its contribution to the housing target is unknown. The practical questions are the cost, safety and quality of the eventual homes, and whether existing residents benefit from the change.

articles.title: Newhey Quarry’s 250-home allocation needs a clearer account of remediation and affordability
articles.excerpt: Newhey Quarry is allocated for around 250 homes, with additional parking intended to support the nearby tram stop. The council’s land assessment classifies the site as brownfield, but the quarry’s history makes its treatment more complicated than simply describing it as unused land.
articles.content_html:
Newhey Quarry is allocated for around 250 homes, with additional parking intended to support the nearby tram stop. The council’s land assessment classifies the site as brownfield, but the quarry’s history makes its treatment more complicated than simply describing it as unused land.

The allocation topic paper records mineral-working consent extending to 2042 and earlier objections that the proposed housing might not match local affordability needs. Those historic records do not establish current extraction activity or a final permission to build homes.

Restoration obligations, ground stability and the definition of previously developed land need to be checked in the actual application. The existence of a quarry alone is insufficient to settle all those issues.

No verified builder, price list or affordable tenure schedule was established in this review. Residents therefore cannot yet be told how many homes will be socially rented or accessible to first-time buyers.

Tram access is a benefit, but it does not establish capacity in schools, GP services, sewers or the local road network. A phased remediation and infrastructure programme will be needed to show that the allocation can become a safe neighbourhood.

The potential 250 homes contribute to the long-term pipeline. They should not be counted as completed housing, nor allocated to an unverified developer’s legal record.

articles.title: Bamford and Norden’s 450-home allocation: housing choice versus pressure on green space
articles.excerpt: The Bamford and Norden allocation envisages around 450 homes alongside improvements to sports and recreation facilities. Its development framework promotes family and affordable housing, but a framework does not establish a completed scheme, a housebuilder’s final layout or an affordable tenancy.
articles.content_html:
The Bamford and Norden allocation envisages around 450 homes alongside improvements to sports and recreation facilities. Its development framework promotes family and affordable housing, but a framework does not establish a completed scheme, a housebuilder’s final layout or an affordable tenancy.

Earlier consultation records document objections about the potential loss of playing fields and pressure on existing sports facilities. Those are recorded community concerns, not evidence that the final scheme necessarily removes those facilities. The council says facilities will be retained and improved through development contributions.

The affordability question remains open. No verified price list, rental schedule or final affordable allocation has been established for a detailed scheme. Describing homes as “high quality” says nothing about whether local households can pay for them.

Infrastructure assessment should address traffic on the surrounding roads, safe walking routes, schools, healthcare and the cumulative effect of other development. The framework’s view that a site is deliverable is not a substitute for funded mitigation attached to a permission.

Until a delivery programme is established, the 450 homes remain potential contributions over time. They should not be represented as homes built this year. A named builder has not been verified, so no builder’s legal history can responsibly be attached to this allocation.

Around half the site is reported as retained for public or open space. School and healthcare capacity still require evidence, and no verified rent schedule or live sales prices were established here.

Taylor Wimpey agreed CMA undertakings in 2021 to remove historic doubling ground-rent terms. Its separate 2025 information-sharing case ended through commitments without an infringement finding. Neither establishes the same issues at Foundry Fields.

The 199 homes belong to the Roch Valley scheme and must not be added to the council’s approximate 200-home allocation as a second development.

Bloor’s Hollingworth Road scheme has been reduced from 312 to 309 homes. Council reporting in June 2026 records site preparation. Developer material includes a central green corridor, sustainable drainage, walking and cycling links and land for a primary school.

Pre-decision reporting identifies 47 affordable homes, approximately 15.2% of the scheme. However, its quoted breakdown of 12 social-rent and 25 shared-ownership homes totals only 37. The school requires careful explanation. Reporting on the planning assessment says population projections did not then justify immediate delivery. Reserving school land is therefore different from promising that a school will open alongside the first houses. The decision must explain funding, demand thresholds and interim provision.

More than 1,000 objections were reported, including concerns about infrastructure. Bloor identifies transport assessments, drainage measures and replacement visitor parking, but the final conditions and funded works determine what will actually be delivered.

Bloor joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

articles.title: Lower Falinge’s proposed 270 homes would replace 150: what residents gain and lose
articles.excerpt: RBH’s next Lower Falinge phase is reported to envisage 270 affordable-rented homes across two parcels, replacing 150 homes proposed for demolition. If implemented on that basis, the eventual net addition is around 120 homes, not 270.
articles.content_html:
RBH’s next Lower Falinge phase is reported to envisage 270 affordable-rented homes across two parcels, replacing 150 homes proposed for demolition. If implemented on that basis, the eventual net addition is around 120 homes, not 270.

The screening-stage proposal includes houses and apartments. It does not itself grant planning permission for the development. The current reference identified in reporting is OTH/2026/0781; final layouts and consent remain separate steps.

There is a directly relevant legal history. Claimants’ barristers reported that the council conceded a challenge to its earlier demolition prior approval over its EIA reasoning. The later October 2025 decision was reported as a refusal. This concerned the decision-making process and should not be recast as a finding of criminal misconduct by a builder.

RBH says regeneration is intended to create safe, warm family homes and has held resident consultation. Existing residents need clear rehousing commitments, costs and any opportunity to return. A temporary loss of homes before replacement is also important for borough-wide supply.

The regulator’s January 2026 judgement confirmed RBH’s G2 governance and V2 viability grades, recognising improvement while identifying risks. It did not assess consumer standards through that stability check.

The infrastructure test must consider the whole regeneration programme and its phases, including services during demolition and reconstruction, rather than treating every parcel as unrelated.

The published material reviewed does not establish the total number of secured affordable homes or their rents. Individual phases must therefore be assessed separately. Northstone’s homes are already within the 1,000-home masterplan and cannot be added again.

Trub Farm is intended to deliver 158 affordable homes through MCI Developments and Legal & General Affordable Homes. Reported plans comprise 48 apartments and 110 houses, with homes for social rent and shared ownership.

The distinction between those tenures is crucial. Social rent is a rental product; shared ownership involves buying a share and meeting additional ongoing costs. Until the final schedule is available, the total should not be described as 158 social-rented homes.

The reporting contains a date discrepancy. An August 2025 article records a committee vote in favour, subject to a legal agreement, while an August 2026 deal article describes approval the previous month. The decision notice and agreement are needed to reconcile a committee resolution with formal permission.

The council committee report identifies open grassland within the urban boundary, adjoining Green Belt rather than simply being described as a Green Belt farm. Its consultation responses require mitigation, but do not establish an already funded expansion in school or GP capacity.

The regulator’s 2026 casework review records strong inspection grades for L&G Affordable Homes and oversight of third-party repairs providers. That provides relevant landlord context, rather than a promise about homes not yet occupied. If delivered, Trub Farm would directly expand affordable options, but exact rents, shares and service charges remain essential missing information.

For the Rochdale fighter, the Glasgow appearance offers an opportunity to make his mark at featherweight and begin a fresh chapter in his BKFC career.

With a new weight class and a determined message to his rivals, Webster will be looking to give his hometown something to celebrate on 7 November.

Now marking their 20th anniversary, the Social Worker of the Year Awards recognise achievements across children’s and adult social work in England. This year, the organisers have named 64 finalists across 14 categories.

Nneamaka is one of six finalists in the newly qualified adult social worker category. The shortlist recognises practitioners at the beginning of their careers, giving Rochdale a representative among those in contention for national recognition.

Gold and silver award recipients will be announced at the October reception.

Rochdale Daily wishes Nneamaka the best of luck.

articles.title: 21 YEARS IN ENGLAND'S BOTTOM 100: Central Rochdale neighbourhood ranked 24th most deprived
articles.excerpt: Government figures show a part of Central Rochdale ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every index since 2004. Where did regeneration funding go — and what can actually be proved about residents' outcomes?
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

A small part of central Rochdale has been ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every national assessment since 2004. In the latest official figures it is 24th out of 33,755 areas — and one of just three places in England to have remained in that bottom 100 across all six releases over 21 years.

The finding is not an opposition-party accusation or a campaign slogan. It appears in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government's English Indices of Deprivation 2025. Its code is E01005482, its statistical name Rochdale 010C, and it falls within the wider Central Rochdale and Mandale Park area.

Official sources: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025 statistical release https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release; Government neighbourhood explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; Government research report https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-research-report

2004. 2007. 2010. 2015. 2019. 2025.

The government's researchers identified only three neighbourhoods that were among the 100 most deprived in every one of those six releases: Rochdale 010C, Middlesbrough 003F and Wirral 011C. The government's research report places the Rochdale neighbourhood within the middle-layer area known as Central Rochdale and Mandale Park.

This is not a description of the whole borough and not even of all Central Rochdale. A Lower-layer Super Output Area is a small census-based statistical area, typically home to around 1,500–1,600 people. The boundary of the LSOA matters when discussing local projects and spending. The Department for Education, for example, locates Whitehall Academy on Whitehall Street inside Rochdale 010C, confirming part of the geography, but the area cannot be equated simply with all of Mandale Park or Rochdale town centre.

Source: Department for Education establishment record for Whitehall Academy, LSOA Rochdale 010C https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/151391

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRIVING THE RANKING?

The 2025 government neighbourhood explorer states that employment deprivation is among the area's most severe problems: fewer than 1% of English neighbourhoods rank as more employment deprived. Rochdale 010C also ranks as the most deprived neighbourhood within the borough for income, with higher-than-usual income deprivation affecting children and older people.

The national index measures seven different types of deprivation: income, employment, education, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, and the living environment. Income and employment carry the largest weights at 22.5% each. In other words, the central issue here is not whether a street looks attractive after regeneration; it is the resources and opportunities available to the people who live there.

Source: Government deprivation explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; methodology and domain weights https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

DOES THIS PROVE THAT ROCHDALE HAS BECOME POORER?

No. The government explicitly warns that deprivation rankings describe RELATIVE circumstances. They do not, on their own, measure absolute changes in poverty, wages, health or household income. Boundaries and methods have changed; the 2025 index includes 55 indicators rather than 39 in 2019. Residents could have experienced improvements while their area's national relative position remained extremely poor.

But staying among the 100 most deprived on six separate occasions is nonetheless compelling evidence of persistent relative disadvantage. A serious assessment of whether interventions worked requires more than a new building or investment headline: longitudinal data on earnings, employment, child poverty, housing quality, health and skills, combined with a clear account of which projects actually reached Rochdale 010C.

Source: Government statistical release and guidance https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

THE REGENERATION MONEY: BIG HEADLINES, BUT WHICH STREETS?

In a 2023 article, Labour council leader Neil Emmott described a £400 million Rochdale town-centre investment programme, including projects such as Riverside, Upperbanks and the restored Town Hall. The council also says the town secured £23.6 million from the government's Towns Fund, intended to support regeneration, skills and connectivity over a wider geographic area. These are genuine funding and development announcements.

Yet neither £400 million nor £23.6 million is an audited total spent exclusively within Rochdale 010C. The figures include a range of projects, investment types, funding sources and locations. Treating either sum as money spent on the approximately 1,600 residents of this one neighbourhood would be misleading.

Sources: Rochdale Council leader's 2023 regeneration statement https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-leaders-blog/investing-future-boroughs-regeneration-continues; council Towns Fund overview https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/business-licensing/towns-fund-money-help-us-improve-rochdale

One more closely relevant entry does appear in Rochdale's formal capital programme: the 2025/26 budget shows £450,000 in external grant funding scheduled for 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale', described as land acquisition and remediation before homes are built by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing and private developers. An earlier programme showed £360,000 scheduled in 2023/24 for the similarly named project.

But these are BUDGET entries, not proof that either amount was actually spent. 'Central Rochdale' is also a broader project designation than LSOA Rochdale 010C. The missing link is a project-by-project ledger with actual expenditure, precise sites, housing completions and beneficiary outcomes.

Sources: Rochdale capital programme 2025/26 to 2029/30, 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale' https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s112547/Append.%201%20for%20Capital%20Programme%20202526%20to%20202930.pdf; 2023/24 capital programme https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s94502/Append.%205%20for%20Budget%20Report%20202324.pdf

WHAT HAS BEEN DONE ABOUT POVERTY?

The council approved 'The Future We Deserve', its borough-wide 2024–2029 anti-poverty strategy, in March 2024. The authority described rising destitution and inequality as reasons for taking a long-term approach. From April 2026 it also began allocating around £5 million in government-backed Crisis and Resilience Fund support across the borough to assist residents facing emergencies, housing pressures and the cost of essentials.

Those programmes matter. They are also different in purpose from capital investment: emergency food and housing support can reduce immediate hardship, while regeneration may seek longer-term jobs and productivity. Neither a borough-wide budget nor a policy document establishes how many residents of Rochdale 010C received support or whether the area's underlying deprivation indicators improved.

Sources: March 2024 Cabinet decision approving anti-poverty strategy https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=55806&Opt=3; council Crisis and Resilience Fund https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund

THE COUNCIL'S OWN RESPONSE TO SOCIAL MOBILITY CONCERNS

In a 2025 response to a social-mobility investigation, Rochdale Council acknowledged significant poverty, deprivation and inequality while pointing to improvements in town centres, education, employment opportunities and transport. It highlighted Rochdale Sixth Form College, Hopwood Hall College, the restored Town Hall and wider development proposals as assets that could improve opportunity.

These represent reasonable arguments for regeneration. But they are evidence of provision and investment, not by themselves proof that low-income residents in Rochdale 010C have entered stable, well-paid work or escaped hardship. This investigation has not obtained an LSOA-specific outcomes evaluation to test that claim.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council response to the Independent Commission on Social Mobility, 2025 https://socialmobility.independent-commission.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Rochdale-Borough-Council-response-to-Deep-dives_-a-local-perspective-on-social-mobility.docx.pdf

WHO SHOULD ANSWER?

Rochdale Council is Labour-controlled, led by Councillor Neil Emmott. The Central Rochdale ward is represented in October 2026 by Councillor Farooq Ahmed (Workers Party of Britain), Councillor Waqar Khan (Workers Party of Britain) and Councillor Sameena Zaheer (Labour and Co-operative), who also holds a Cabinet portfolio for Corporate, Governance and Transformation. The ward is a different boundary from the statistical neighbourhood and its current councillors did not all serve throughout the 21-year period.

These affiliations identify democratic responsibility and representation; the deprivation index does not establish misconduct, negligence or causation by any individual councillor or political party.

Sources: Council councillor directory https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7214; https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=5385; Workers Party councillor directory https://www.workerspartygb.org/our_councillors; council control https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/councilmeetings

SEVEN QUESTIONS THAT DESERVE DOCUMENTED ANSWERS

1. Which completed, current and planned projects since 2004 have physically overlapped the boundary of LSOA E01005482?

2. For each project, how much public funding was approved, contracted and actually spent — separated from private investment and borough-wide allocations?

3. What proportion of jobs created or safeguarded under those programmes went to residents of this exact neighbourhood, and at what wages?

4. How have child income deprivation, employment deprivation, housing conditions and school attendance changed in absolute terms over time, not merely national rankings?

5. What specific measurable targets did the 2024–2029 Anti-Poverty Strategy set for the most deprived neighbourhoods, and how does Rochdale 010C perform against them?

6. What data will the council use to demonstrate that forthcoming developments are benefiting the people already living in this neighbourhood, rather than simply changing the appearance or population mix of nearby streets?

7. Will the council publish an independently auditable, geographically itemised account of 20 years of spending and outcomes, and allow residents to examine the results?

WHY IT MATTERS

Rochdale's new shops, college provision, housing developments, town-hall restoration and cultural attractions are visible and can produce genuine benefits. The government's latest deprivation statistics show a different and equally important side of local economic life: one neighbourhood has remained among England's most deprived in every national index for more than two decades.

That is not proof that £400 million was wasted. It is proof that the success of regeneration cannot be established from the value of construction projects alone. The ultimate test is whether residents gain lasting opportunities, better homes, improved health and higher disposable incomes.

Rochdale Daily is inviting the council, its regeneration agency, the ward councillors, relevant public bodies and local community organisations to provide a full geographic spending-and-outcomes breakdown and their responses to these findings.
